https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cy5d.text: Image source, EPA Image caption, Smoke rises above a Wildberries facility following a reported Ukrainian drone strike at the Koledino Industrial Park near Podolsk in Russia on Sunday By Tabby Wilson Published 18 August 2026, 02:16 BST Updated 1 hour ago Russia has accused the UK of "deliberately opting for an escalation of the Ukraine crisis" following confirmation that British-made drones had been used in strikes on targets in Russia. "In doing so, the United Kingdom is acting as an accomplice and co-perpetrator of the bloody crimes and terrorist attacks," the Russian Embassy to the UK wrote in a statement. "London's actions will inevitably carry consequences for which it will have to answer," it said, adding that the deeper its involvement in the conflict, "the higher the price it will pay". In response, a spokesperson for the Ministry of Defence (MoD) told BBC News that Britain stood "shoulder to shoulder" with Ukraine. "Russia should be in no doubt about the resolve of this Government to stand against Russian aggression, in Ukraine and against the UK and our allies," said the spokesperson in a statement. The UK, they added, was "committed to providing the equipment Ukraine needs to defend itself against [Russian President Vladimir] Putin's illegal invasion". Built by two separate British companies, the drones in question have been used inside Russia in widespread and successful targeting of military and industrial targets, including refineries and warehouses of the online retailer Wildberries. Ukraine has repeatedly targeted the company, known as Russia's version of Amazon, and says that seven out of 10 of the largest Wildberries logistics centres have been "disabled". A military source confirmed to the BBC that UK drones had been used in the attacks, which are said to have caused more than Â£35bn in economic damage. Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and currently controls approximately a fifth of Ukrainian territory. Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has said drones using UK components and configurations were used to attack Russian territory, including a fuel depot in the Kamensky District of the Rostov Region. UK-made drones strike targets inside Russia Published 1 day ago Russia and Ukraine trade more deadly strikes Published 17 hours ago Russian ship defies sanctions to send military vehicles to Mali Published 2 August How Ukraine is taking the war 'deeper' into Russia Published 6 August Moscow's warning to the UK comes after a wave of Ukrainian strikes on Russia. In the latest attacks overnight, Russian officials said some 620 drones had been flown towards the region surrounding Moscow. Russian air defences destroyed more than 180 of the drones but several people were left wounded, the officials said. An attack the night before saw nine people killed and 23 injured, including a child. On Saturday night, Ukraine fired some 822 drones towards Russia, with 600 aiming for Moscow, according to its regional governor, who said the Russian capital had suffered "one of the most massive drone attacks in recent memory". Seven deaths were reported across Russia. On the same night, Russian attacks on Ukraine killed at least seven people and injured more than 39. In April, the MoD announced it would supply Ukraine tens of thousands of drones, including long-range strike devices, in its biggest ever package. following flash floods â official updated E ELTA, LRT.lt 2026.08.26 15:57 Nepal flash floods. | AP A Nepalese tourism official said Wednesday tourists from Lithuania were among the missing foreign nationals following devastating flash floods in the country. âPreliminary data from tourism and travel agencies show that 384 travellers are missing in the affected areas, including 291 foreign nationals and 93 Nepalese citizens,â the Nepal Tourism Board said, adding that authorities were working to establish the whereabouts of the travellers. Santos Panta, director of the Nepal Tourism Board, told the dpa news agency in Kathmandu on Wednesday that most of the missing foreign tourists were from India, but that travellers from several other countries, including the United States, Spain, Lithuania and Germany, were also unaccounted for. The flooding hit an area where the popular Langtang Valley trekking route begins, as well as other areas visited by Hindu pilgrims. A police spokesman said earlier that authorities did not yet know the full extent of the damage, but warned people living near the river to move to safer areas. 'We have no information' â MFA Lithuania's Foreign Ministry said on Wednesday it had no information about Lithuanian travellers missing in floods in northern Nepal, despite reports in Nepalese media suggesting some may be among the missing. "The Embassy of the Republic of Lithuania in India is aware of the case, and the situation in the affected region is being monitored. At this time, we have no information regarding missing or injured citizens of the Republic of Lithuania," the ministry said on Wednesday. The ministry said consular officials were prepared to provide all necessary assistance to Lithuanian citizens should such requests be received. At least 19 people died on Wednesday during a major flood near the border with Tibet, while hundreds of tourists, including Lithuanian nationals, remained unreachable. https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/worl.text: In the small city of West, Texas, a annual celebration of Czech heritage began in 1976 as a modest fundraiser to support the local community. What started as a single day of polka music, kolaches and a hometown parade has grown over five decades into one of the stateâs most beloved cultural festivals. In 2026, the year of Westfestâs 50th anniversary, couples who had been married during the first year of the festival returned to march in the parade, now as grandparents, surrounded by their children and grandchildren. As KWBU reported , the milestone highlighted how a community event rooted in immigrant traditions can become a multigenerational touchstone, uniting families and neighbors over the span of half a century. A small town with deep Czech roots West, Texas, is located on Interstate 35 between Dallas and Austin, a place where the smell of baking kolaches often welcomes visitors before they even cross the town limits . The area was settled in the late 19th and early 20th centuries by Czech and Slovak immigrants who arrived in search of land and opportunity .They brought with them their language, Catholic faith, folk music, dance and recipes that would become defining features of the community.For generations, Czech identity in West was lived in everyday ways. Families spoke Czech at home, attended mass at the local Catholic church, and gathered for weddings, funerals and holidays that followed old country customs. Over time, English became dominant and younger generations drifted toward broader American culture, but the markers of Czech heritage remained strong, especially in food, music and community celebrations.The birth of a festivalIn the mid 1970s, community leaders in West were looking for ways to raise funds for local projects and to strengthen civic pride. They decided to organise a festival that would celebrate the townâs Czech roots while drawing visitors from across the region. The first Westfest was held in 1976, featuring a parade, live polka bands, traditional dance groups, food booths and a queen pageant. Kolaches, klobasy and other Czech inspired foods were front and centre, offering a taste of the townâs culinary heritage.The event was an immediate success. Residents turned out in force, and visitors from nearby towns and cities came to experience the music, food and small town atmosphere. What began as a fundraiser quickly became an annual tradition, with each year building on the last. The parade grew longer, the crowds larger and the programming more elaborate, but the core focus on Czech culture and community remained unchanged.Fifty years of music, food and traditionOver five decades, Westfest has become a fixture on the Texas cultural calendar. The festival now spans multiple days, with events that include a grand parade, royalty coronation, carnival rides, craft vendors, 5K runs and continuous performances of Czech and polka music. Dance troupes in folk costumes perform traditional routines, passing down steps and songs that were once common in village squares in Bohemia and Moravia.Food remains a central draw. Local bakeries and vendors sell thousands of kolaches, fruit filled pastries that have become synonymous with Czech Texas. Savory klobasy, roast chicken and other specialties are prepared in large quantities, often using recipes that have been in families for generations. For many attendees, the taste of a fresh kolach is inseparable from the memory of past festivals, family gatherings and childhood visits to West.The parade is the emotional heart of the celebration. Local schools, church groups, civic organisations and businesses march alongside classic cars, fire trucks and floats that reflect both Czech themes and contemporary community life. Grand marshals are often chosen for their long service to the town or their connection to the festivalâs history. Over the years, the parade has documented the changing face of West, from agricultural roots to a more diversified economy, while maintaining a strong sense of continuity.A homecoming for the class of 1976The 50th anniversary of Westfest in 2026 offered a natural moment for reflection. Organisers reached out to residents who had been part of the first festival, including couples who were married in or around 1976. Many of these couples had attended Westfest throughout their lives, first as young adults, then as parents bringing their own children to the parade and dances.For the golden anniversary, several of these couples returned to march in the parade as grandparents, accompanied by their children and grandchildren. Some wore sashes or carried signs noting their 50 years of participation. Others just walked together, pointing out landmarks along the route and telling stories of how the festival had changed and remained the same. For them, Westfest was not just an event but a timeline of their lives, marking milestones like marriages, births, graduations and losses. Seeing multiple generations walk side by side in the parade made the passage of time visible in a way that few other local traditions do. Teenagers who had once ridden on floats now pushed strollers. Former festival queens watched their own granddaughters compete in the pageant. The continuity was both personal and communal, a reminder that the festivalâs endurance depends on families choosing to return year after year.Keeping heritage alive in a changing worldWestfestâs survival is genuinely impressive at a time when small-town festivals everywhere are folding. Between shifting demographics, digital distractions, and volunteer burnout, keeping an annual tradition alive is tough work. West also had to endure far deeper trauma after the tragic 2013 fertilizer plant explosion that devastated the community and killed fifteen residents.Yet the festival survived by striking a smart balance between tradition and fresh energy. Organizers modernized the event by bringing in bigger carnival rides, diverse live music, and active social media marketing to draw in younger families. At the same time, they kept the heart of the festival untouched, continuing the solemn memorial mass, authentic Czech folk dancing, and beloved homemade recipes.Beyond the local economic boost, Westfest keeps a unique heritage alive for the next generation. Kids grow up learning traditional dances, catching snippets of the Czech language in songs, and connecting specific foods with family celebrations. Even if they never become fluent, they walk away with a deep sense of identity and pride in where they come from.More than a celebrationFor many in West and the surrounding region, Westfest is more than a weekend of events. It is a reunion, a homecoming and a reaffirmation of community ties. People who have moved away often plan their year around the festival, returning to reconnect with relatives, friends and neighbours. Local businesses count on the influx of visitors, and civic groups use the occasion to fundraise and recruit volunteers.The 50th anniversary underscored how deeply the festival is woven into the fabric of local life.When couples who were married in 1976 walked the parade route with their descendants, they were not just celebrating a milestone. They were embodying the festivalâs original purpose, to bring people together around shared heritage and shared place. In doing so, they offered a vision of what Westfest might look like at 75 or 100 years, with new generations taking up the same roles their grandparents once held.Looking to the next 50 yearsAs the 2026 celebration concluded, organisers and residents alike looked ahead. The challenge will be to keep Westfest vibrant and relevant while preserving the traditions that make it unique. That will mean continuing to welcome new families, supporting local Czech culture and finding ways to honour the past without being trapped by it.If the first 50 years are any guide, the festival has a strong foundation. It began as a fundraiser and became a institution. It survived disasters and demographic shifts. It grew from a single day into a multi day event that draws tens of thousands of visitors. Most importantly, it remained a place where families could see their own stories reflected in the parade, the music and the shared meal of a warm kolach on a Texas autumn day.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/24/isra.text: Israeli forces pushed into the West Bank city of Hebron on Saturday and displaced up to 250 families, some in the middle of the night, vowing a heavy price over a deadly attack on two soldiers.Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said he was planning an operation on a scale not seen since Israel first occupied the West Bank in 1967. The lockdown comes after Palestinian militants killed two Israeli soldiers on Friday at a checkpoint near Hebron, a flashpoint city in which hardline Israeli settlers live surrounded by local Palestinians.The operation is taking place just days before Israel is set to hold elections on Tuesday, in which Netanyahu is expected to face a tight race with the opposition bloc led by former military chief Gadi Eisenkot.In the neighbourhood of Ein Dir Baha nestled between two hills, buildings were marked by X's showing they had been cleared of people.The streets in the area were deserted of people and cars other than Israeli military vehicles. Around one-third of Hebron has been targeted, local Governor Khaled Dudin told news agency AFP."They started in the neighbourhood from which the people who carried out the attack came, but there is no guarantee that the operation will not expand," he said. "This amounts to collective punishment being imposed on civilians who have nothing at all to do with this," he said.The governor said 150 families had been affected, while the mayor of Hebron, Youssef al-Jaabari, and local activist Issa Amro put the figure at 250."We will find them shelter and provide these people with all the help they need," the mayor told AFP.Israel promises further action in the run-up to Tuesday's general electionThe Israeli military said it was "conducting precise, targeted and thorough searches" focused on the area of the two gunmen, who were both killed in the gunfight.It said the operation would last several days, in line with similar army actions after previous attacks.Prime Minister Binjamin Netanjahu's far-right national security advisor, Itamar Ben Gvir, has called on Israel to dismantle the Palestinian Authority, the semi-autonomous body that governs parts of the West Bank in cooperation with Israel under 1990s peace accords.Asked if he agreed on destroying the Palestinian Authority, Netanyahu, Israel's longest-serving prime minister, boasted that he has rejected pressure from three US presidents to work to establish a Palestinian state.Taxis piled up behind gates controlled by Israel's military outside Hebron, waiting for Palestinians who are forced to cross on foot. All gates leading in and out of the city were closed to vehicles, according to Basma Radio, a Telegram channel Palestinians use to monitor checkpoints and road closures.Israel's army didn't respond to questions about the operation. On Friday, it said that in response to the killing of two soldiers and wounding of others, its forces had begun “conducting precise, targeted and thorough searches” in the area of Hebron from which the two gunmen had operated.Rights group Yesh Din reported 672 incidents of settler violence over the past 26 days, nearly half related to the olive harvest, an annual event with cultural resonance to Palestinians that extremist settlers have sought to stop.Polls show Netanyahu neck and neck with an opposition bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot, a centre-right former military chief who also opposes a Palestinian state but has promised to crack down on settler violence.
